ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: A certain pond has two populations, zooplankton and algae, and the trend of their population densities changing over time is shown in the figure. If a large number of a certain kind of fish (C) that feeds exclusively on zooplankton is put into the pond, after a period of time, only one population will remain among the three populations A, B, and C in the pond. Which population will it be?

Which population will it be?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the vertical axis is labeled “population density”, and the horizontal axis is labeled “time”. There are two periodically fluctuating curves: the solid line is labeled A, and the dashed line is labeled B. In each round of fluctuation, the peak of A appears before the peak of B, and the change of B lags behind A. Reasoning: The pond originally has zooplankton and algae. In a predation relationship, the number of the prey usually increases first, and then the number of the predator increases, so A, which reaches the peak first, should be algae, and B, which reaches the peak with a lag, should be zooplankton that feeds on algae. After a large number of fish C that feeds exclusively on zooplankton is introduced, C will prey heavily on B, causing the number of zooplankton B to decrease or even disappear; afterward, C will also be unable to maintain itself and disappear due to lack of food. Algae A loses the feeding pressure from zooplankton and will ultimately remain. Therefore, the only remaining population is population A.
